title: Marathi Cinema Just Had Its Best Month Ever. Two Films. ₹140 Crore. And Bollywood Watched.
excerpt: Raja Shivaji broke Sairat's decade-old record. Deool Band 2 came from nowhere. May 2026 belongs to Maharashtra.
body:
In the same month that Bollywood's biggest releases limped to underwhelming totals, Marathi cinema did something unprecedented: it produced two concurrent blockbusters that collectively grossed over ₹140 crore worldwide. One broke a record that had stood for a decade. The other was a devotional drama that nobody saw coming.

Raja Shivaji: The Record-Breaker

Riteish Deshmukh directed and starred in Raja Shivaji, a historical epic about the life of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj. The film opened on May 1 and has not stopped running. In 26 days, it has crossed ₹114 crore worldwide — officially surpassing Sairat's ₹110 crore lifetime to become the highest-grossing Marathi film of all time.

The significance of dethroning Sairat cannot be overstated. Nagraj Manjule's 2016 drama didn't just hold the record; it defined it. For a decade, ₹110 crore was the ceiling that Marathi cinema could aspire to but never breach. Multiple films tried — Baipan Bhari Deva (₹90.5 crore), Ved (₹73 crore), Natsamrat (₹46 crore) — and all fell short.

Raja Shivaji didn't just clear the bar. It did so with weeks of theatrical runway still ahead. Trade analysts are projecting a final total of ₹120-130 crore, which would place the film in a category no Marathi film has ever occupied.

The film features Sanjay Dutt and Abhishek Bachchan in supporting roles, produced by Genelia Deshmukh and Jyoti Deshpande under the Mumbai Film Company and Jio Studios banners. Its Hindi-dubbed version alone contributed ₹29 crore — nearly as much as many standalone Hindi releases earn in total. That crossover is telling: Shivaji Maharaj's story, told in Marathi, connected with audiences who don't speak the language.

Deool Band 2: The Surprise Nobody Expected

If Raja Shivaji was the film everyone was watching, Deool Band 2 was the film nobody expected to matter. The devotional drama opened to a modest ₹2.90 crore and, by every historical metric, should have disappeared within a week.

Instead, it went the other way. Positive word-of-mouth sent audiences back. Weekend growth was strong. Weekday holds were remarkable. In just six days, the film had already crossed ₹26.50 crore and is now marching toward ₹50 crore — blockbuster territory for a film of its scale and marketing budget.

Bollywood's Contrast

The timing makes the Marathi success even more striking. May 2026 saw two high-profile Hindi releases — Pati Patni Aur Woh Do (starring Ayushmann Khurrana) and Chand Mera Dil (from Dharma Productions) — both underperform badly. PPAWD managed ₹53.85 crore worldwide after weeks in theatres; Chand Mera Dil stalled at ₹21 crore in five days.

The box office table for May tells the story more cleanly than any analysis can. The top three Indian films released in May — Karuppu (Tamil, ₹253 crore), Drishyam 3 (Malayalam, ₹170 crore), and Raja Shivaji (Marathi, ₹114 crore) — are all regional. The highest Hindi entry is fourth.

What This Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs, particularly the Maharashtrian diaspora, Raja Shivaji is a cultural event. Screenings in New Jersey, the Bay Area, and London have drawn strong audiences. The film taps into a pride that goes beyond cinema — Shivaji Maharaj occupies a space in the Marathi imagination that is as much spiritual as historical.

But the broader lesson matters for every Indian language community abroad: regional cinema no longer needs Bollywood's permission to be commercially viable. Raja Shivaji proved it by outselling Hindi films in Hindi-speaking markets. Deool Band 2 proved it by building an audience purely on word of mouth.

May 2026 will be remembered as the month Marathi cinema stopped being a niche and started being a force.
nri_angle: Maharashtrian NRIs are driving strong overseas numbers for Raja Shivaji. The broader shift toward regional cinema dominating Hindi markets is reshaping what Indian films the diaspora sees on screens abroad.
author: Diaspora Desk
